data.title: ADR-003: Zero runtime dependencies in the core
body: # ADR-003: Zero runtime dependencies in the core
After ADR-001, 160 ms is left for all the CLI's work. The cost of the `import` alone was measured for the candidates (best of 3, Node v25.8.2, without bundling):
`zod` alone costs 15% of the entire budget — for validating an object with seven fields.
So the cost of our own implementations of the same thing was measured:
| Own implementation | Import cost | Throughput | Correctness |
| ULID (26 chars, Crockford base32) | **0 ms** | 100k in 132 ms | sorting by time — yes; 50k unique with no collisions |
| Event validation (7 fields, type guards) | **0 ms** | 100k in 17.5 ms | catches all 6 classes of error |
| `zod` for the schema + `ulid` | The schema as the single source of types; an implementation proven by the community | 33.7 ms of import together — 21% of the budget for ~60 lines of functionality |
| `valibot` for the schema | Modular, tree-shakable, 5 ms | We still pay for a general-purpose engine where the shape of an event is fixed and does not change at runtime |
| Own ULID + validation | 0 ms; full control; no CVEs and no updates in the supply chain | ~60 lines that have to be covered by tests and maintained by us |
**The core (modules M1–M5) has no runtime dependency whatsoever.** ULID and event validation are our own, under tests.

This is not "not invented here". There is exactly one argument and it is measurable: general-purpose validation libraries are built for schemas that are described at runtime and change. Here the shape of an event is fixed in the types at compile time, and the check is needed exactly at the boundary — when we read a file that a human or a merge could have corrupted. For that task a 5.8 MB engine gives nothing that a 20-line function does not, while costing a fifth of the startup budget.

ULID was chosen (instead of UUIDv4) for a separate reason: the first 10 characters are a timestamp in Crockford base32, so lexicographic sorting of the identifiers coincides with chronological order. The order of events becomes a property of the ID itself and does not depend on how far the system clocks on different machines have drifted apart — this directly closes the edge case from section 7.3 of the PRD.
- Positive: ~34 ms of the budget saved; `npm audit` on the core has nothing to show; the supply chain consists of zero links.

- Cost of the decision: ~60 lines of cryptographically sensitive (ULID uses `node:crypto`) and validation code — our duty to test. Both implementations have to be covered by property tests, not only by examples.

- What will have to be reconsidered: if the event schema becomes extensible by plugins (user-defined event types with their own fields), fixed validation will stop working — then we return to `valibot` as the cheapest of the engines.
